We want to understand what you meant by "I’m not certain if that specific placement aligns with our current internal guidelines just yet", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The order summary section is placed at the very top of the checkout page, above the payment details section.

B) The total amount is made visually prominent within the order summary, while the item details and subtotal sit around it in the same top section.

C) The checkout layout groups the order summary and payment details as separate stacked sections, with action areas positioned below them.

D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.
turns.a: C is probably closest to what I meant. I was reacting to the way the order summary and payment details are stacked as separate cards, and then the main actions sit underneath as their own area. That may be perfectly fine, but from a project or process standpoint I’d want to check whether the expected checkout flow is summary first, payment second, then actions, because the buttons at the bottom also create a pretty strong sequence.

turns.q: Looking at the layout, what specifically makes the order summary, payment details, and action areas feel like separate stacked sections rather than one connected checkout flow?
turns.a: I think it’s the card boundaries and spacing doing most of that. The order summary is in its own bordered white panel, then there’s a gap, then Payment Details is another bordered white panel, and then the buttons sit outside both cards on the gray page background. Also, “Continue Shopping” is the strongest visual action because it’s the black filled button, while “Place Order” is disabled-looking and separated below it, so the flow feels less like one checkout path and more like three separate blocks the user has to interpret.

turns.q: How does the bordered-block styling and the visual weight of “Continue Shopping” versus “Place Order” contribute to the checkout feeling fragmented?
turns.a: The bordered blocks sort of make each part feel like a self-contained module: first “ORDER SUMMARY,” then “Payment Details,” and then a separate button zone, rather than one continuous path toward purchase. What stands out to me now is that the black “Continue Shopping” button has much more authority than the pale gray “Place Order” button, so visually the page seems to be encouraging exit or reversal more than completion. From a project delivery perspective, I’d probably flag that as a requirement question, not just a design preference: is the primary user outcome supposed to be finishing payment, because the hierarchy here doesn’t quite say that.

turns.q: What design decision in the button styling and section framing makes “Continue Shopping” read as the primary action while “Place Order” feels secondary?
turns.a: The big thing is that “Continue Shopping” is the only high-contrast filled control on the page: black background, white label, full width, and it sits immediately after the payment card. “Place Order” uses a pale gray fill with low-contrast gray text, which is the pattern people often read as disabled or unavailable, even if that wasn’t the intent. The section framing reinforces that because both the order and payment parts are boxed, but the actual checkout decision is outside those boxes, so the first strong standalone button becomes the one that feels like the recommended next step.
